Act! meets QuickBooks

Getting a sales team and an accounting system to agree about money, without either one lying to the other.

UX & Interaction Design · Scherry Sweeney Designed with an AI agent August – September 2026
01 · The problem

Two systems, one customer, and a lot of retyping

A small business wins work in Act! and gets paid in QuickBooks. Today, nothing connects those two facts except a person with two browser tabs open.

A quote is accepted. Somebody opens QuickBooks and types the invoice in again — the customer, the line items, the amounts, the dates. When the money arrives, they type it back the other way, or more often they don't, and Act! quietly stops reflecting reality.

The cost isn't the typing. It's that the two systems disagree, and nobody knows which one to trust. A salesperson calls a customer who paid last week and asks for money. Someone chases an invoice that was settled. A business owner looks at their pipeline and their bank balance and cannot reconcile them.

What we set out to build

When a quote is accepted in Act!, a draft invoice appears, ready to review. Send it, and it becomes a real invoice in QuickBooks. When the customer pays, the payment comes back to Act! on its own. Nobody types anything twice, and both systems agree.

02 · Who we designed for

Four people, four completely different jobs

Every screen was designed against four named people doing a real task. They want opposite things from the same data, which is most of why the design took the shape it did.

Dana PrenticeBilling

Bills the work and chases the money. Opens Act! on a Tuesday to clear the queue, and needs to know an invoice really exists before she moves on.

03 · The main screen

The queue that turns accepted work into money

This is the surface the whole feature is built around. Every quote a customer has accepted, waiting to be billed — with the oldest and the most urgent at the top, because that is the order a person actually works in.

04 · Design thinking

The decisions that were hard

A feature that moves money is mostly a study in what to do when things go wrong. These are the four calls that shaped everything else.

1 · When a send fails, say what did not happen

QuickBooks can refuse an invoice — a tax code it doesn’t recognise, a customer record it won’t accept. The obvious design shows the error. The useful design answers the question the person is actually asking, which is "did it half-work?"

Somebody whose send just failed is not worried about the tax code. They are worried they have just billed a customer twice. So the screen says nothing was created before it says anything else, then quotes QuickBooks word for word rather than paraphrasing — because the fix is in QuickBooks, and a paraphrase is not searchable.

Most of the design work on this page is about a path that fails rather than one that works. The failure paths were taken as seriously as the happy one — which is usually the difference between a feature people try and a feature people keep.

2 · A blank screen has three completely different meanings

An empty list can mean there is nothing to do, we cannot reach the data, or it hasn’t arrived yet. Most software draws one blank screen for all three. That is how a person concludes their work is done when it is merely invisible.

So we drew all three and made them impossible to mistake for one another. The empty one is a success. The unreadable one refuses to show a count at all, because a zero is a claim. The third keeps the table’s own shape while it waits, rather than throwing the layout away behind a spinner and making everything jump when the data lands.

3 · The salesperson who must never touch an invoice

Marcus closes deals. He should never send an invoice, and he should never have to ask whether one went out. When his quote is accepted the draft builds itself, and a banner appears on the deal telling him three things: what state it is in, that nothing has been sent yet, and who will send it.

It is the smallest surface in the feature and one of the most carefully worded. Everything it says is designed to stop him doing something — and to stop him worrying that nobody else will.

4 · A trial that shows you the value and withholds the button

On a free trial the integration connects, pulls in a year of real invoices and payments, and builds drafts from accepted quotes. Everything works — except the one button that sends.

That is a deliberately uncomfortable design, and it was argued about. Hiding the feature teaches a trial user nothing. Letting them send would put real invoices into a real customer’s books from an account that has not paid for it. So the design shows the whole machine running, with the last step held back and the reason stated where the button would be.

The wording does the work: "not yet", never "you cannot". What is in the queue on the day you subscribe is ready to go.

A screen is not one picture. Each of these had to be designed for every state a person can land on — connected, disconnected, empty, failing, loading, permitted, denied, on a trial, mid-send.

06 · Designing with an AI agent

What each of us was actually good at

This was designed in partnership with an AI agent rather than in a drawing tool. It is a genuinely different way to work, and worth reporting honestly — the division of labour turned out to be sharper, and less obvious, than expected.

What the agent made possible

Speed at a scale that changes what is feasible. 123 fully considered states in fourteen working days — roughly nine a day, each one drawn, written, and checked against the rest of the set. A team drawing these by hand would have scoped the feature down to fit the calendar. Nothing had to be cut for time.

Consistency no person can hold. When a status changed, all 123 states could be re-checked against the new rule in minutes. That is where real defects come from — the fourth screen nobody remembered to update.

The written record wrote itself as we went. The reasoning behind each decision was captured at the moment it was made rather than reconstructed later, which is the only time it is accurate.

Tooling became free. A suite of 33 automated checks, four clickable walkthroughs built straight from the screens, a live map of the whole set, and this page — each cost an afternoon instead of a week, so each one actually got made.

Breadth without fatigue. Cross-referencing sixty open questions against a 22,500-word record, every time, without getting bored and skipping one.

What the designer brought

Product judgement — what to build and what to refuse. Three tabs or two. A flat ledger or a grouped one. Show the trial its own value or hide the feature. Every decision in section 04 was a human call; the agent held its consequences steady across 123 screens.

Eyes. The agent cannot see. Every judgement about whether something looked right came from a person opening the screen — and real defects were caught that way, including a tile that rendered as if it had failed to load.

Domain knowledge the agent had no access to. What our platform can actually do, what production already looks like, which patterns exist, what Act!’s users expect. An early screen built on an aspirational shell had to be reverted on exactly this.

Knowing which question to ask. Short, sceptical questions — "am I missing it?", "didn’t we already decide this?" — caught several confident, well-argued, wrong answers in seconds. Not reviewing the output: interrogating the reasoning.

Priority and a stopping rule. A design this size yields a finding on every pass. Deciding which ones matter — "fix only what would make someone build the wrong thing" — is what let the work be called finished instead of polished forever.

Knowing the room. What to send, to whom, and when. Which arguments were worth having and which were noise.

The agent is extraordinary at consistency and useless at taste. Knowing which is which is the whole skill.
07 · What we learned

Six things worth carrying to the next one

  1. 01Count the states before setting the date The arithmetic above was available on day one for the price of an hour's counting, and it is a far better basis for a plan than a guess about how long design "should" take. Count the work, then set the date — not the other way round.
  2. 02Split the build plan by what it depends on Five of the eight workstreams needed nothing from design at all and could start immediately — and did, with no friction. The three that describe screens are worth holding until the screens exist. Same amount of parallel work, without the rework.
  3. 03Requirements should say what, not how A requirements document that also contains the build plan starts going out of date the moment design begins — and design always changes things, because that is what design is for.
  4. 04Agree early what the mockups are for Reference for a rebuild, or the thing that ships? It changes how much precision is worth buying, and it is a one-sentence conversation at kickoff.
  5. 05Give design a way to see all of it at once Working through an agent meant 123 states were described in conversation and never assembled anywhere a person could stand back and look. We built that map eventually. It took about an hour and should have existed in week one.
  6. 06Check the claim before you send it Anything leaving design should point at the thing that proves it. Speed in a status update is worth nothing if somebody else has to verify it.
